Nomura: The Midterm Elections Won't Help, Only the Fed CanmarsbitPublished on 2026-11-01Last updated on 2026-11-01AbstractNomura strategist Naka Matsuzawa argues that the U.S. midterm elections will not be the catalyst that ends the global tech selloff, contrary to widespread market hopes. In his October 30 macro strategy note, he contends that election results matter far less to equities than expected, and that the only real catalyst capable of halting the tech decline is the Federal Reserve ending its rate-hiking cycle.

Matsuzawa attributes tech weakness not to election uncertainty but to two deeper drivers: mounting concerns over the sustainability of AI investment and persistent credit worries. He notes that event premiums around the midterms in futures markets have already fallen noticeably, and that companies expected to face tighter regulation have not visibly underperformed—evidence that the selloff is not directly tied to regulatory fears. Investors, he observes, are punishing earnings misses harshly while giving little credit to beats, and they favor restrained capex, improved cash flow and shareholder returns over aggressive spending, reflecting deep anxiety about an AI investment slowdown.

Recent sector moves—a rebound in semiconductors (SOX up 6.9% for the week) alongside weakness in hyperscalers and software—do not, in his view, constitute meaningful rotation, since capital goods and machinery stocks, typically leading indicators of AI investment recovery, remain subdued. bonuses.requirements: Goldman Sachs Raises U.S. Data Center Construction Spending Forecast to $125 Billion by 2028HomeFeedNewsGoldman Sachs Raises U.S. Data Center Construction Spending Forecast to $125 Billion by 2028Goldman Sachs Raises U.S. Data Center Construction Spending Forecast to $125 Billion by 202811/07 11:40Despite market panic triggered by stricter data center regulations following the Democratic Party's control of Congress, Goldman Sachs has raised its forecast for U.S. data center construction spending, increasing the 2026 estimate from $67 billion to $80 billion, and the 2027 estimate from $87 billion to $100 billion. For the first time, it projects that spending will reach $125 billion in 2028. Goldman Sachs noted that there are currently about 86 GW of data center projects under construction in the U.S., with an additional $900 billion in high-confidence projects awaiting construction, indicating that the overall construction cycle remains resilient. The demand from major cloud service providers like Microsoft, Amazon, and Google, along with backlogged orders, has not shown significant signs of cooling, with H100 computing power rental prices up 26% year-on-year and GB200 rental prices rising 50% since the beginning of the year. Regarding the data center moratorium proposed by Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, Goldman Sachs believes its impact will be more about delaying project deliveries rather than directly canceling construction plans, although it could lead to increased financing costs, reduced tax incentives, and some clients canceling contracts.
